## The APE code and the NACE classification

Every business registered in France receives an **APE code** (*activité principale exercée*, principal activity). This code places the unit in the French activity classification, the **NAF** (*nomenclature d'activités française*), which is the national version of the European **NACE**. It is attached to the business's identifiers in the **Sirene** register, which INSEE has managed since 1973 and which is the legal reference for the SIREN and SIRET numbers.

The APE code is not just an administrative label. It is used to:

- build the sampling frames of business surveys and the structural business statistics;
- produce national accounts and short-term indicators broken down by industry;
- apply sector-specific regulation (collective agreements, insurance, some taxes and grants).

A coding error therefore spreads into statistics as well as into the administrative life of the business.

The classification is hierarchical, with five levels:

| Level | NAF rev. 2 (2008) | NAF 2025 (NACE Rev. 2.1) |
|---|---|---|
| Sections | 21 | 22 |
| Divisions | 88 | 87 |
| Groups | 272 | 287 |
| Classes | 615 | 651 |
| Sub-classes (APE code) | **732** | **746** |

: Size of the NAF classification at each level. Upper levels for NAF 2025 follow NACE Rev. 2.1. {#tbl-naf}

::: {.callout-note}
## What we predict
The target is the **sub-class**, the finest level, with about 750 possible labels. The higher levels follow directly from the code, so metrics are reported at every level of the hierarchy.
:::

## From a structured form to free text

Each time a business is created or changes its activity, it files a declaration that includes a description of its activity. Until 2022, a clerk at a business formalities centre helped the declarant fill in the form, so activity descriptions were fairly short and standardised.

Two reforms changed this:

1. **The PACTE law (2019)** set up a **single online one-stop shop** (*guichet unique*), run by INPI. Since 1 January 2023, all business formalities go through it. The activity description became a free-text field, typed by the declarant with no one to help.
2. **Sirene 4**, the new information system of the register, moved from nightly batch processing to **continuous processing** built on micro-services. The migration was gradual, starting at the end of 2022.

As a result, texts are longer, more verbose and more varied. They also include all the spelling quirks you would expect from free input.

Each year, about **2 million** descriptions must be coded.

## Three generations of coding engines

| Period | Engine | Principle | Limits |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1990s → 2022 | **Sicore** | Deterministic rules, keyword dictionaries | The automation rate fell to about 30 % on free-text descriptions. The rules were costly to maintain. |
| End of 2022 → 2025 | **fastText** | Supervised model (bag of words and character n-grams), with auxiliary variables added to the text as tokens | Meta archived the library in March 2024. It offered no calibration, no explainability and no GPU support. |
| 2025 → | **PyTorch** ([torchTextClassifiers](companion-projects.qmd#sec-ttc)) | Same family of models, rebuilt in PyTorch: a dedicated embedding per categorical variable, calibration, explainability | Inference is somewhat slower than fastText, but still within budget. |

: Successive APE coding engines. {#tbl-history}

**Sicore** was developed in the 1990s [@meyer1997]. It handled the well-structured texts of the former system well, but on free-text descriptions it automated only about one case in three. The rest, about 70 %, had to be coded by hand [@avouac2025].

The **fastText** model went into production gradually from November 2022, with a deliberately conservative threshold at first. It brought the automation rate back to around **80 %**, which made the one-stop-shop reform workable.

When Meta archived the fastText repository in March 2024, the team started moving to **PyTorch**. The move was also an opportunity to fix the model's structural weak points: how categorical variables were handled, calibration, and explainability. The result is the open-source package torchTextClassifiers, described in [Companion projects](companion-projects.qmd).

## Production constraints

The model is called by the Sirene information system for each declaration as it arrives. This sets strict constraints:

- **Unit inference on CPU** in a closed environment: no GPU, no internet access, and every dependency shipped with the model.
- **Low latency**: the target is about 200 ms for each call.
- **Fallback to a human**: the model returns its five most likely codes, each with a probability, plus a **confidence index**. Below a threshold, the declaration goes to a manual coding team, who see the model's suggestions.
- **Traceability**: every prediction must be linked to the exact version of the model that produced it.

The **automation rate** is the share of declarations coded with no human involvement, at a controlled level of accuracy. It is the key business indicator, because it determines the workload of the manual coding teams.

## Why MLOps

A model trained once and never touched again does not stay good for long, for several reasons:

- the way declarants describe their activity drifts over time, as new trades, new legal forms and new phrasings appear;
- business experts report errors that must be fixed quickly and permanently;
- the classification itself changes: the move from NAF rev. 2 to NAF 2025 required recoding the entire training set (see [Data](data.qmd#sec-naf2025));
- the libraries the model depends on get deprecated (fastText) or move to new major versions (MLflow, PyTorch).

The rest of this note describes the system that makes this work routine: reproducible training, a versioned model registry, an API deployed through GitOps, continuous monitoring and annotation, and a retraining protocol with explicit quality gates.
